title: Cracking the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional
subtitle: Study strategy, domain breakdown, and the mental models that helped me pass the hardest AWS certification on the first attempt.
overview: The AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional (SAP-C02) is widely regarded as one of the most demanding cloud certifications available. It demands not just service knowledge but the ability to weigh trade-offs, design across multiple AWS accounts and regions, and make architecture decisions given business constraints. This article walks through how I structured my preparation — what I studied, how I organised the domains, and the mental models I used to reason through the scenario-heavy exam questions.
problem: The SAP exam is not a memory test — it is a reasoning test disguised as one. Questions present complex, multi-service architectures and ask you to choose between options that all technically work, but differ in cost, operational overhead, scalability, or resilience. Passing requires internalising the *why* behind each service, not just its name and feature list. My notes spanned three broad pillars: Security & Compliance, Networking & Compute, and Data & Analytics. Structuring study around these pillars rather than individual services made the concepts stick.
architecture:
Study pillars mapped to exam domains:

Pillar 1 — Security & Compliance
  IAM (Policies, Roles, Federation, STS)
  KMS, CloudHSM, SSM, Secrets Manager
  CloudTrail, AWS Config, GuardDuty
  Shield, WAF, ACM, SNI
  S3 encryption, access points, Object Lambda

Pillar 2 — Networking & Compute
  VPC (subnets, IGW, NAT, NACL, SG)
  Transit GW, VPC Peering, PrivateLink
  Direct Connect, S2S VPN, Client VPN
  Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator
  Load Balancers (ALB/NLB/GwLB/CLB)
  ECS, EKS, Lambda, App Runner
  API Gateway, AppSync, Step Functions

Pillar 3 — Data & Analytics
  RDS, Aurora, RDS Proxy
  DynamoDB, DAX, ElastiCache
  Kinesis Streams, Firehose, Analytics
  Redshift, Athena, Glue, EMR
  SQS, SNS, Amazon MQ, MSK
  AWS Batch, DocumentDB

implementation.title: Pillar 1 — Security: IAM, Federation, and KMS
implementation.description: IAM is the spine of every AWS architecture. The key mental model: every action is allowed or denied by evaluating policies in a specific order — Service Control Policies → Resource-based policies → IAM identity policies → Permission boundaries → Session policies. Federation bridges corporate identity into AWS: SAML 2.0 with ADFS is the enterprise on-premises path, AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) is the modern replacement. Web Identity Federation with Cognito adds per-user IAM policy scoping that raw Web Identity without Cognito cannot do.
implementation.code:
# IAM policy evaluation order (denial wins at every layer)
# 1. Explicit Deny anywhere → DENY
# 2. SCP (Org-level) doesn't Allow → DENY
# 3. Resource-based policy Allows → ALLOW (cross-account)
# 4. Identity-based policy Allows → ALLOW
# 5. Permission boundary doesn't Allow → DENY
# 6. Session policy doesn't Allow → DENY

# SAML 2.0 Federation (legacy)
User → Corporate IdP (ADFS) → SAML Assertion → STS AssumeRoleWithSAML → Temp Creds

# Modern: IAM Identity Center (SSO)
User → IAM Identity Center → AWS account access (no STS wiring needed)

# Web Identity with Cognito (mobile/web apps)
User → Login (Google/FB) → Cognito → STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity → Scoped temp creds
# Cognito adds: user pool management, per-user IAM policy, token refresh

implementation.title: Pillar 1 — Security: KMS, CloudHSM, Secrets, and Parameter Store
implementation.description: Encryption service choice is a favourite exam topic. KMS manages keys in software (shared multi-tenant HSMs). CloudHSM gives you dedicated single-tenant hardware — needed for SSL offloading and FIPS 140-2 Level 3 compliance. SSM Parameter Store is for non-secret config; Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation, which Parameter Store alone cannot do. The exam often asks: use Secrets Manager for DB passwords with rotation, SSM SecureString for config that doesn't rotate.
implementation.code:
# KMS key types
Symmetric  → AES-256, single key for encrypt+decrypt, never leaves KMS
Asymmetric → RSA / ECC, public key downloadable, private key in KMS

# When to use what
KMS            → general-purpose encryption, S3/RDS/EBS at-rest
CloudHSM       → SSL/TLS offloading, FIPS Level 3, bring-your-own key control
SSM Param Store → app configs, feature flags, non-rotatable secrets (free tier)
Secrets Manager → DB passwords, API keys — auto-rotation via Lambda, costs $/secret

# CloudTrail audit trail
API Call → CloudTrail (90d free) → S3 (long-term) or CloudWatch Logs (alerting)
Paid: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API call volume anomalies
Pattern: CloudTrail → EventBridge rule → SNS → PagerDuty alert

implementation.title: Pillar 1 — Security: Shield, WAF, and DDoS architecture
implementation.description: DDoS attacks fall into four buckets: volumetric (UDP flood), protocol (SYN flood), DNS amplification, and application layer (slow HTTP). Shield Standard covers layers 3/4 for free on all AWS resources. Shield Advanced adds layer 7, cost protection, and DDoS response team. WAF operates at layer 7 only — attach it to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, or AppSync. The exam loves the separation pattern: put static assets on S3/CloudFront (no EC2 attack surface), put dynamic APIs behind ALB+WAF.
implementation.code:
# DDoS protection layers
Layer 3/4 (network/transport): AWS Shield Standard (free, automatic)
  - Protects against SYN floods, UDP reflection, volumetric attacks

Layer 7 (application): AWS WAF (paid, rules-based)
  - Attach to: CloudFront | ALB | API Gateway | AppSync
  - Rules: IP block lists, rate limiting, SQL injection, XSS

# Architecture for DDoS-resilient public site
Internet → Route 53 (health checks, failover)
         → CloudFront (Shield + WAF + Geo restriction)
         → S3 (static assets) | ALB (dynamic API) → EC2 Auto Scaling Group

# SNI — multiple SSL certs on one IP
Server Name Indication: client sends hostname in TLS handshake
→ ALB and CloudFront select the correct ACM certificate per domain
→ CLB does NOT support SNI (only one cert)

implementation.title: Pillar 2 — Networking: VPC fundamentals
implementation.description: VPC design is tested heavily. The key distinctions: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic automatic) and attach to instances/ENIs. NACLs are stateless (must allow both inbound and outbound explicitly) and apply to subnets. VPC Peering is not transitive — A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C. Transit Gateway solves this with a hub-and-spoke model connecting hundreds of VPCs and on-prem networks. PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Interface) exposes a service privately without VPC peering — the consumer never sees the provider's VPC.
implementation.code:
# VPC traffic flow (public subnet)
EC2 → Route Table → IGW → Internet

# NAT Gateway (private subnet outbound only)
EC2 (private) → Route Table → NAT GW (public subnet) → IGW → Internet
# NAT GW is AZ-scoped — deploy one per AZ for HA

# Connectivity comparison
VPC Peering    → 1-to-1, non-transitive, same or cross-account/region
Transit GW     → hub-and-spoke, transitive, attach VPCs + VPNs + Direct Connect
PrivateLink    → expose service via NLB, consumer uses ENI endpoint, no peering needed
VPC Endpoint GW → free, S3 and DynamoDB only, routes via route table

# On-premises connectivity
S2S VPN → Customer GW + Virtual Private GW, encrypted over public internet
         Static routing (CGW side) or dynamic BGP
Direct Connect → dedicated private line, not encrypted by default, lower latency
Client VPN → OpenVPN for remote employees into VPC

implementation.title: Pillar 2 — Compute: Lambda, ECS, and load balancers
implementation.description: Lambda constraints are exam staples: 15-min timeout, 128MB–10GB RAM, 1000 concurrent executions (soft limit), /tmp 10GB, sync payload 6MB, async 256KB. For DB connections from Lambda use RDS Proxy — Lambda creates thousands of concurrent connections, RDS Proxy pools them so the DB isn't overwhelmed. Load balancer selection: CLB is legacy; ALB is Layer 7 with path/host-based routing and targets EC2, ECS, Lambda, IP; NLB is Layer 4 for high throughput TCP/UDP; GwLB is Layer 3 for inline third-party appliances like firewalls.
implementation.code:
# Lambda limits to memorise
Timeout          : 15 min max
Memory           : 128 MB – 10 GB (CPU scales with memory, not selectable)
Concurrency      : 1,000 default (request increase for prod)
Reserved conc.   : hard cap per function, prevents noisy-neighbour
/tmp storage     : 10 GB (ephemeral, per invocation)
Sync payload     : 6 MB request + 6 MB response
Async payload    : 256 KB

# RDS connection pooling with RDS Proxy
Lambda (1000 concurrent) → RDS Proxy → RDS (limited connections)
# Proxy maintains persistent pool; Lambda connects to proxy, not DB directly

# Load balancer quick reference
CLB → legacy, Layer 4 OR 7, single SSL cert only
ALB → Layer 7, HTTP/2, WebSocket, path/host routing, Lambda target, WAF
NLB → Layer 4, TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency, static IP, preserve client IP
GwLB → Layer 3, GENEVE protocol, inline traffic inspection (firewalls/IDS)

# Cross-zone load balancing
Enabled by default: ALB (no charge), GwLB (charged)
Disabled by default: NLB (charged if enabled)

# API Gateway limits
Timeout: 29 seconds (hard limit — Lambda must complete within this)
Max payload: 10 MB

implementation.title: Pillar 2 — Networking: Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator
implementation.description: These three are often confused. Route 53 is DNS with health checks and routing policies (latency, geolocation, weighted, failover). CloudFront is a CDN — it caches content at edge locations and reduces origin load. Global Accelerator is not a CDN — it routes TCP/UDP traffic over the AWS backbone via anycast IPs, cutting latency for non-cacheable workloads like gaming or real-time APIs. The exam distinguishes: use CloudFront for static/cacheable; use Global Accelerator for dynamic, latency-sensitive, non-HTTP.
implementation.code:
# Route 53 routing policies
Simple        → one record, one destination
Weighted      → split traffic by % (blue-green, canary)
Latency       → route to lowest-latency region
Failover      → primary/secondary with health check
Geolocation   → by country/continent
Geoproximity  → by distance + bias shift (Traffic Flow required)
Multivalue    → up to 8 healthy records returned (not load balancer replacement)

# CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
CloudFront       → CDN, caches at edge PoPs, HTTP/S, reduces origin requests
Global Accelerator → No caching, anycast IP → backbone → regional endpoints
                     Use for: gaming, VoIP, IoT, multi-region failover

# CloudFront security
Signed URLs      → single file, time-limited access (S3 pre-signed is different)
Signed Cookies   → multiple files, maintains session
Geo Restriction  → allowlist/blocklist by country (CloudFront, not WAF)
OAC              → Origin Access Control replaces OAI for S3 origins
Lambda@Edge      → runs Node.js/Python at edge PoP (viewer/origin request/response)
CF Functions     → JS only, lighter, cheaper, viewer-side only

implementation.title: Pillar 3 — Data: DynamoDB, Aurora, and caching
implementation.description: DynamoDB is the exam's favourite NoSQL. Key patterns: TTL for auto-expiry, Streams for change-data-capture into Lambda, DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for microsecond read latency on hot keys. ElastiCache sits above DAX for computed/aggregated results — DAX caches raw DynamoDB items, ElastiCache caches anything. Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible with shared distributed storage, 15 read replicas, 30-second failover, up to 128TB auto-scaling. RDS Multi-AZ is synchronous standby for HA; Read Replicas are asynchronous for read scaling — these are different.
implementation.code:
# DynamoDB key numbers
Throughput : 1 million RPS (provisioned or on-demand)
Item size  : max 400KB
Streams    : 24h retention, ordered per-partition, triggers Lambda
TTL        : attribute-based expiry, no WCU consumed
DAX        : write-through cache, microsecond reads, cluster in VPC

# Caching decision tree
Hot DynamoDB items          → DAX (purpose-built DynamoDB cache)
Computed/session/aggregated → ElastiCache Redis (sorted sets, pub/sub, persistence)
Simple cache, no replication → ElastiCache Memcached (multi-thread, no persistence)

# Aurora vs RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas
RDS Multi-AZ     → sync standby, auto-failover, SAME region, NOT for reads
RDS Read Replica → async copy, CAN be cross-region, promotes to standalone DB
Aurora           → shared distributed storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs
                   15 RRs, 30s failover, cluster endpoint auto-routes writes
Aurora Serverless → auto-scales ACUs, idle pause, good for intermittent workloads
Global Aurora    → 1 primary region, up to 5 read-only regions, <1s replication lag
                   Write Forwarding: secondary regions forward writes to primary

implementation.title: Pillar 3 — Data: Kinesis, SQS/SNS, and messaging
implementation.description: Streaming vs queuing is a key distinction. Kinesis Streams retains data (default 24h, up to 365d) and supports replay — multiple consumers can re-read the same data. SQS deletes a message once consumed — no replay, but simpler. Kinesis Firehose is a managed delivery pipeline to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch — near-real-time (buffered), no retention. SNS fan-out pattern: one SNS topic → multiple SQS queues, each consumed by different services independently.
implementation.code:
# Kinesis Streams — shards and throughput
Producer: 1 MB/s or 1,000 msg/s per shard
Consumer (shared): 2 MB/s per shard, max 5 GetRecords calls/s
Consumer (enhanced fan-out): 2 MB/s per shard per consumer, push model
Retention: 24h (default) → 7d → 365d
Replay: YES — seek to any position in the stream

# Kinesis Firehose
Destinations: S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, MongoDB, Splunk, Datadog, HTTP endpoint
Latency: near-real-time (60s buffer or 1MB min)
Retention: NONE — delivery only

# SQS key properties
Standard: at-least-once, best-effort ordering, unlimited throughput
FIFO: exactly-once, strict ordering, 3,000 msg/s with batching
Visibility timeout: hides message while consumer processes
DLQ: after N failures, moves to dead-letter queue for inspection
Long polling: reduces empty receives, up to 20s wait
Delay queue: postpone delivery up to 15 min (good for retry backoff)

# Fan-out pattern
S3 Event → SNS Topic → [SQS Queue A → Lambda A]
                     → [SQS Queue B → Lambda B]
                     → [SQS Queue C → Email subscriber]

implementation.title: Pillar 3 — Analytics: Athena, Glue, Redshift, and EMR
implementation.description: The analytics stack is frequently tested as architectural choices. Athena is serverless SQL on S3 — pay per data scanned, so partition data and use Parquet/ORC with 128MB+ files to minimise cost. Glue provides the Data Catalog (schema registry) that Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR all read from. Redshift is a columnar OLAP data warehouse for sustained BI queries. Redshift Spectrum runs queries against S3 without loading data in, using the Redshift cluster for compute. EMR runs Hadoop/Spark on managed clusters — EMRFS stores data in S3 (not HDFS) for durability.
implementation.code:
# Analytics service selection
Serverless SQL on S3         → Athena (pay per TB scanned)
ETL + schema registry        → AWS Glue (catalog reused by Athena, Redshift, EMR)
Columnar data warehouse      → Redshift (sustained BI, OLAP, MPP)
S3 query without ingestion   → Redshift Spectrum (Redshift cluster + S3 data)
Big data / Spark / Hadoop    → EMR (managed, EMRFS=S3 backed)
Document / MongoDB workload  → DocumentDB

# Athena cost optimisation
1. Use columnar format: Parquet > ORC > CSV (reads only needed columns)
2. Partition by date/region — scan only matching partitions
3. Compress files: Snappy, GZIP
4. Target file size ≥ 128 MB (too many small files = more overhead)

# Glue data catalog
Glue Crawler → auto-discovers schema → Data Catalog
Data Catalog → shared by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR (no schema duplication)
Glue ETL     → serverless Spark jobs, Python or Scala, triggered by EventBridge

# Redshift Workload Management (WLM)
Queue per workload type (ETL vs BI vs ad-hoc)
Short-query acceleration (SQA) for fast queries
Concurrency scaling adds transient clusters on burst

implementation.title: Study strategy and exam approach
implementation.description: The SAP exam contains 75 questions in 180 minutes (~2.4 min/question). Questions are scenario-based and often 200+ words long. Most wrong answers are technically correct but fail on one dimension: cost, operational overhead, scalability, or resilience. The best study pattern: read question → eliminate obviously wrong → compare remaining on the single axis the question is really testing. Flag uncertain questions and revisit. Time is tight — practice reading fast.
implementation.code:
# Study plan (8–10 weeks, ~2h/day)
Weeks 1–2  : IAM, KMS, VPC fundamentals (security + networking base)
Weeks 3–4  : Compute — Lambda, ECS, EKS, API Gateway, load balancers
Weeks 5–6  : Database — RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache
Weeks 7–8  : Analytics — Kinesis, SQS, SNS, Glue, Athena, Redshift
Weeks 9–10 : Practice exams, weak areas, re-read AWS whitepapers

# Key whitepapers to read
- Well-Architected Framework (all 6 pillars)
- Disaster Recovery whitepaper (RPO/RTO targets → Backup/Pilot/Warm/Active-Active)
- Security best practices
- Storage options

# Exam day tips
- Mark and skip long questions, come back with fresh eyes
- "Most cost-effective" → usually serverless or managed (not EC2)
- "Least operational overhead" → fully managed service wins
- "Highly available" → Multi-AZ, cross-region, auto-scaling
- "Least data loss" → sync replication (Multi-AZ, not Read Replica)
- When two answers seem equal, check: does one require you to manage infra?

impact: AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional issued October 2022 by Amazon Web Services
Validated ability to design solutions across 40+ AWS services with business context trade-offs
Hands-on architecture patterns applied directly to production systems: Kinesis pipelines, Aurora Global, Lambda + SQS fan-out, VPC PrivateLink
lessons: Study services in clusters, not individually — IAM, STS, and Cognito only make sense together; Kinesis Streams and Firehose only make sense when you contrast them
The exam tests trade-off reasoning, not trivia — for every service, know when NOT to use it as much as when to use it
Operational overhead is its own dimension — a technically correct answer that requires you to manage EC2 fleets will lose to a managed-service answer at the SAP level
Practice exams expose gaps faster than re-reading notes — do them early, not just at the end, and treat wrong answers as the actual study material
Whitepapers on DR (RPO/RTO), Well-Architected pillars, and security best practices are not optional — several questions are direct extracts from them
